problem: Complex Subset Sum: Given n complex numbers with sum of norms = 1, prove there exists a subset S with |sum_S z_k| >= 1/6.

gold_atoms.trigger: Problem involves complex numbers but the constraint and objective only depend on norms and sums — suggests geometric viewpoint
gold_atoms.action: Recast complex numbers as 2D vectors; the problem becomes: from unit-total-length vectors, find a subset whose vector sum has large norm
gold_atoms.outcome: Problem is now purely geometric, enabling directional/projection arguments
gold_atoms.boundary: Fails when the problem genuinely needs complex-analytic structure (e.g., roots of unity arguments, analytic continuation). In this case geometry suffices.

gold_atoms.step: Small case analysis to diagnose structure
gold_atoms.trigger: Extremal/optimization problem where the difficulty is unclear
gold_atoms.action: Test n=1, n=2 to identify what makes the problem hard
gold_atoms.outcome: Reveals that cancellation between vectors is the core obstacle — full sum can be small, need to select a subset avoiding cancellation
gold_atoms.boundary: Small cases guide intuition but don't prove the general case. Fails when behavior changes qualitatively at larger n.

gold_atoms.step: Factor the constant to find proof architecture
gold_atoms.action: Interpret each factor as a separate loss: 1/3 from pigeonhole on 3 sectors, 1/2 from projection onto bisector
gold_atoms.outcome: Two-stage proof plan: (1) select a good sector, (2) bound the projection within that sector
gold_atoms.boundary: Heuristic — fails when the constant is not cleanly factorable or when factors don't correspond to independent losses. Also only gives 1/6, not the optimal 1/4 or 1/pi.

gold_atoms.trigger: Need to select a subset of vectors that don't cancel; vectors span all directions
gold_atoms.action: Partition the plane into k equal sectors. By pigeonhole, some sector contains vectors with total norm >= 1/k. Take those vectors as the subset.
gold_atoms.outcome: A subset is selected where all vectors point roughly the same direction (within angle 2pi/k)
gold_atoms.boundary: The bound from just pigeonhole is 1/k, and projection within the sector loses a factor of cos(pi/k). Optimizing k gives k=4 (quadrants) with bound 1/4. Does NOT give the optimal 1/pi — for that, need the continuous averaging method.

gold_atoms.step: Projection onto bisector to get scalar bound
gold_atoms.trigger: Have a subset of vectors all within angle 2pi/k of each other; need a lower bound on |sum|
gold_atoms.action: Project all vectors onto the sector bisector. Since all angles are within pi/k of the bisector, each projection retains at least cos(pi/k) of its norm.
gold_atoms.outcome: The real part along the bisector is >= cos(pi/k) * (total norm in sector), giving the final bound
gold_atoms.boundary: Projection is lossy — you throw away the component perpendicular to the bisector. For k=3 the loss is cos(pi/3)=1/2, giving 1/6. For k=4 it's cos(pi/4)=sqrt(2)/2, giving 1/4.

gold_atoms.trigger: Discrete sector methods give sub-optimal constants; want the best possible bound
gold_atoms.action: Instead of k fixed sectors, average over ALL directions alpha in [0, 2pi). For each alpha, take the subset S_alpha = {k : Re(z_k e^{-i*alpha}) >= 0}. The average over alpha of the real part of sum_{S_alpha} equals (1/pi) sum |z_k|.
gold_atoms.outcome: By averaging argument, there exists alpha_0 achieving at least the average, giving bound 1/pi
gold_atoms.boundary: Requires computing integral of max(cos(u), 0) over [0, 2pi] = 2. This is a pure computation — should be delegated to CAS. The averaging method needs a continuous symmetry group (rotations); fails for discrete/combinatorial settings without continuous symmetry.

gold_atoms.trigger: Averaging argument produces an integral that determines the constant
gold_atoms.action: DELEGATE TO CAS: compute integral_0^{2pi} max(cos(u), 0) du = 2
gold_atoms.boundary: Pure computation — no mathematical insight, just mechanics. Risk of error if done in tokens.
